lead: A microwave resonator stores electric and magnetic energy and returns it at one frequency, f0. Energy sloshes between a capacitor and an inductor, or in the fields of a cavity or line section. Q, the quality factor, compares energy stored with energy lost per radian. High Q gives a narrow response; low Q gives a broad one. Resonators sit inside filters, oscillators, duplexers and frequency meters — every block that picks one frequency and rejects the rest.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for distributed L and C, 1.3 for the input impedance of shorted and open lines, and 1.7 for waveguide modes.

blocks.text: A series RLC circuit has impedance Z = R + j(ωL − 1/(ωC)), where R is resistance in ohms, L inductance in henries, C capacitance in farads and ω = 2πf the angular frequency in rad/s. At one frequency the reactances cancel: ω0L = 1/(ω0C). The impedance drops to R and current peaks. That is resonance.

blocks.where: f0 is the resonant frequency in hertz, L is inductance in henries, C is capacitance in farads.

blocks.text: A parallel RLC circuit is the dual. At the same f0 its admittance is minimum, so impedance and voltage peak. Both circuits are resonators: they store energy and give it back.

The sharpness of that peak is Q, the quality factor. In words, Q = ω0 × (energy stored) ÷ (power lost). A lossless circuit has infinite Q and a spike; a lossy one has finite Q and a rounded peak. Q also equals f0 divided by the 3 dB bandwidth, so a sharp peak and a narrow bandwidth are the same statement.

blocks.where: ω0 = 2πf0 in rad/s, W is the energy stored in joules, P_loss is the power lost in watts.

blocks.text: For a series circuit Q = ω0L/R = (1/R)√(L/C); for a parallel circuit Q = Rp/(ω0L) = ω0RpC, with Rp the shunt resistance in ohms. A large series R spoils Q; a small shunt Rp spoils it. Every resonator is an L–C pair plus one loss resistance.

A real resonator is connected to a source and a load. Three Q values describe it. Q0, the unloaded Q, counts only internal losses: metal resistance, dielectric loss, radiation. Qe, the external Q, counts only power leaking through the coupling. QL, the loaded Q, counts both. They combine like parallel resistors.

blocks.where: QL, Q0 and Qe are dimensionless quality factors: loaded, unloaded and external.
f0 is the resonant frequency in hertz and BW is the 3 dB (half-power) bandwidth in hertz — the width over which the response stays above 1/√2 = 0.707 of its peak.

blocks.text: A QL of 100 at 2 GHz means a 20 MHz bandwidth. High QL means a narrow passband; low QL a wide one. The same number says how long stored energy survives: after the drive is removed the amplitude decays as exp(−t/τ) with τ = 2QL/ω0. High-Q resonators ring for many cycles — welcome in an oscillator, unwelcome in pulse radar.

items: Q0 fixes the best bandwidth the resonator could ever give.
Qe fixes how strongly it is coupled to the outside world.
QL is what you measure on a network analyser, and it is always lower than Q0.

blocks.text: Below about 1 GHz a resonator is a coil and a capacitor. At 10 GHz the needed L and C are so small that the coil is a fraction of a millimetre and its resistance destroys Q. Microwave design therefore uses distributed resonators, where a line or metal box stores the energy.

λ/2 resonator. A line of length l = λ/2 shorted at both ends has zero input impedance at f0: a series resonance. The same length open at both ends has infinite input impedance: a parallel resonance. Harmonics appear at every multiple of f0.

λ/4 resonator. A shorted stub of length λ/4 shows infinite input impedance at its open end — it behaves as a parallel resonant circuit. A physical short becomes an electrical open. An open λ/4 stub is the dual and shows a series resonance.

blocks.where: c is the speed of light in the filling medium in m/s, a, b, d are the cavity width, height and length in metres, and m, n, p are the mode indices (TEmnp or TMmnp).

blocks.text: A closed metal box is a waveguide with walls at both ends. Only certain field patterns fit, so it is a rectangular cavity resonator with these frequencies. It is large, so Q of a few thousand is easy. Q grows with the volume-to-surface ratio and falls as surface resistance Rs = √(πfμ/σ) grows, where f is frequency in hertz, μ is permeability of the metal in henries per metre and σ is conductivity in siemens per metre.

items: Dielectric resonator: a ceramic puck of εr between 20 and 40, with Q set by loss tangent, Qd = 1/tan δ, often several thousand. Small enough to sit on a printed board.
Microstrip resonator: a printed λ/2 open line. Q is modest, tens to a few hundred, because fields touch lossy dielectric and thin metal.
Temperature drift: f0 moves as the box warms, quoted as a temperature coefficient of frequency in ppm/°C. A near-zero coefficient holds frequency; an uncompensated high-Q cavity does not.

figure.caption: The response peaks at f0 and falls to 0.707 of the peak at f/f0 = 0.995 and 1.005, a fractional bandwidth of 1/QL = 1% for QL = 100.

spec.aria: A resonator response peaking at f/f0 equal to 1 and falling to 0.707 at f/f0 equal to 0.995 and 1.005 for a loaded Q of 100.

examples.question: A bandpass resonator is centred at f0 = 2 GHz. Its 3 dB bandwidth measured on a network analyser is 20 MHz. (a) Find the loaded Q. (b) The unloaded Q of the resonator alone is 500. Find the external Q and comment on the coupling.
steps: Check the fractional bandwidth: BW/f0 = 20 MHz ÷ 2000 MHz = 1%, and 1/QL = 0.01, so the two agree.
Qe (125) is much smaller than Q0 (500): coupling is strong, external loss dominates, and QL (100) is well below Q0. Loosening the coupling raises Qe, pulls QL up toward 500 and narrows the bandwidth.
examples.check:
f0 = 2e9
BW = 20e6
Q0 = 500.0
QL = f0/BW
Qe = 1.0/(1.0/QL - 1.0/Q0)
print(QL)
print(Qe)

traps: Using Q0 in QL = f0/BW when the resonator is connected. The measured bandwidth belongs to QL, not Q0.
Writing Q = BW/f0. Q is f0/BW, so wide bandwidth means low Q.
Calling a shorted λ/4 stub a series resonance. Its input impedance is infinite, so it is parallel; a shorted λ/2 line gives series resonance.
Forgetting Q0 and QL differ, and that loaded Q must be smaller than unloaded Q.
Assuming a high-Q cavity is frequency-stable. Temperature drift moves f0; exams ask for bandwidth from QL and drift in kHz.

quiz.q: Define the quality factor of a resonator in terms of stored energy and power loss.
quiz.a: Q = ω0 × (energy stored) ÷ (power lost), where ω0 = 2πf0 is the resonant angular frequency in rad/s. For a series circuit Q also equals ω0L/R.

quiz.q: Write the resonant frequency of an ideal LC resonator and name each symbol.
quiz.a: f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), with f0 in hertz, L in henries and C in farads.

quiz.q: Why does a high loaded Q mean a narrow bandwidth?
quiz.a: QL = f0/BW, so BW = f0/QL. For a fixed f0, raising QL shrinks the bandwidth. Physically, high Q means little energy is lost per cycle, so the resonance responds only over a small band around f0 and decays slowly in time.

quiz.q: A resonator resonates at 5 GHz with a loaded Q of 250. Find its 3 dB bandwidth. If its unloaded Q is 1000, find the external Q.
A rectangular cavity has a = 3 cm, b = 1.5 cm and d = 4 cm, air filled. Find the resonant frequency of the TE101 mode.
Using Zin = jZ0 tan(βl) for a shorted lossless line, explain why a shorted λ/4 stub acts as a parallel resonance and a shorted λ/2 line as a series resonance.
quiz.a: At l = λ/4, βl = π/2 and tan(βl) → ∞, so Zin → ∞: an open circuit, which is parallel resonance. At l = λ/2, βl = π and tan(βl) = 0, so Zin = 0: a short circuit, which is series resonance. The physical termination has not changed; only the electrical length has.

quiz.q: A printed microstrip resonator and a copper cavity are both designed for 5 GHz. Explain why the cavity has the far higher Q, and state one advantage of the microstrip version.
quiz.a: The cavity confines the fields in air inside a large metal volume, so conductor loss is spread over a large surface and dielectric loss is absent; Q reaches thousands. The microstrip resonator squeezes its fields into a thin dielectric and thin metal, so conductor and dielectric loss are both high and Q is only tens to a few hundred. The microstrip version is cheap, small and made on the same board as the rest of the circuit.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, cavity filters in cellular base stations hold Q above 5000 and pass one channel. Dielectric-resonator and thin-film bulk-acoustic resonators set frequency in phone front-ends. Superconducting cavities reach Q above 10⁹ and serve particle accelerators and quantum computing, where photon lifetime τ = 2QL/ω0 must hold a qubit state.
